notes.meaning: God commands Moses to make the inner room of the tabernacle with ten beautiful curtains. These curtains are made of fine linen dyed blue, purple, and scarlet, with figures of heavenly beings called cherubim woven right into the fabric. The figures show that God's angels surround His dwelling and watch over His people. Because the Israelites live in tents in the desert, God chooses a tent as His home so He can travel right with them.

Each curtain is about forty-two feet long and six feet wide, making them all identical in size. Five of the curtains are sewn together into one wide sheet, and the remaining five are sewn into a second sheet. Making them in two large sets makes the heavy material much easier to pack up and carry through the wilderness.

Fifty loops of blue cord are fastened along the edge of each large sheet, perfectly lining up with one another. Fifty gold clasps then hook the loops together to join the two sheets into one single cover over the tent. This joining shows how God knits His people together in love and peace so they become one united house for Him.

Next, God tells Moses to make eleven curtains from dark goats' hair to form an outer tent over the inner linen dwelling. This coarse cloth is tough and protects the delicate, colourful inner curtains from rain and desert dust. From the outside the tent looks plain, but on the inside it is rich and glorious, just as God values a quiet, faithful heart far more than outward show.

Each goats' hair curtain is forty-five feet long and six feet wide, which is slightly longer than the inner linen curtains. Five of them are sewn into one set, and six into another. The sixth curtain is folded in half at the front entrance of the tent, hanging like a neat border or veil over the door.

Fifty loops are placed on the edge of each goats' hair sheet, just like on the inner curtains. Instead of gold, fifty bronze clasps link the loops together to make the covering a single unit. Bronze is a plainer and tougher metal, well suited to hold together this sturdy outer layer.

Because the goats' hair covering is longer and wider than the linen layer beneath it, extra fabric hangs down around the sides and back. The extra folded section covers the rear wall, and an extra foot and a half hangs down each side. This ensures that the costly and delicate linen layer underneath is fully sheltered from wind, sun, and dirt.

Two more outer coverings are placed on top of the goats' hair tent. The first is made from ram skins dyed red, and the final top layer is made from durable leather. These heavy outer skins shield the sacred wooden frame and beautiful tapestries from the scorching desert sun and blowing sand.

A sturdy wooden frame is built to hold up the heavy coverings like walls. These upright boards are made of acacia wood, which grows in the desert and lasts a very long time. Each board stands fifteen feet high and over two feet wide.

Each wooden board has two wooden pegs carved at the bottom, placed side by side. These pegs fit neatly into heavy metal bases on the ground. This clever design lets the workers set up the walls firmly and take them down quickly when it is time to move camp.

The south wall of the tabernacle uses twenty of these upright boards. Underneath them sit forty heavy silver bases, with two bases supporting each board to receive its two wooden pegs. These silver bases keep the wooden frame stable and lift it off the dirt floor.

The north wall is built in the exact same way as the south wall. It has twenty upright acacia boards resting on forty silver bases, two under every board. This symmetry gives the sanctuary strength and balance on both sides.

The back of the tabernacle faces west and is closed off with six wooden boards. Two extra boards are specially made for the two rear corners to tie the sides and the back firmly together. Since the entrance faces east toward the rising sun, the back wall turns worshippers away from sun-worship toward the true God.

The corner boards are paired together tightly from the bottom to the top and locked into a single ring. In all, the back wall has eight boards standing on sixteen silver bases. These strong corner pieces brace the whole structure so it will not sway or collapse.

Wooden crossbars made of acacia wood run horizontally to lock the upright boards into solid walls. Five bars are made for the north wall, five for the south wall, and five for the back wall. The middle bar runs all the way from one end of the wall to the other, holding every board tightly in place.

All the wooden boards and crossbars are covered with thin sheets of shining gold, and gold rings are attached to hold the bars. Inside the tent, the walls look entirely like solid gold reflecting the light of the sacred lamps. This royal splendour reminds the priests that they are standing in the palace of the great King of heaven.

God commands Moses to set up the tabernacle following the exact model he saw on Mount Sinai. Every measurement and material has a purpose given by God. It shows that true worship is not left to human guesswork, but follows what God Himself has revealed.

Moses is instructed to make a thick, beautiful inner curtain called the veil, woven with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen. Figures of cherubim are skillfully worked into it. This veil hangs from gold hooks on four gold-covered acacia posts set in four silver bases, acting as a royal screen before God's throne room.

The veil is hung under the clasps of the ceiling curtains to divide the tent into two rooms. The outer room is called the Holy Place, and the inner room is called the Most Holy Place, where the sacred Ark of the Covenant is placed. This barrier warned people that human sin kept them from coming directly into God's holy presence, until Jesus died and tore that barrier away.

Inside the Most Holy Place, the golden mercy seat is placed directly on top of the Ark of the Covenant. Outside the dividing veil, in the Holy Place, the table of bread sits on the north side, and the golden lampstand stands across from it on the south side. The light from the lampstand shines across the room onto the bread of God's presence.

At the front entrance of the tent, an embroidered screen is made of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen. It hangs on gold hooks across five gold-covered acacia pillars resting in sturdy bronze bases. This hanging serves as the only doorway into God's tent, showing that only those whom God invites and cleanses may draw near to Him.
